source_text:
Πολλὰ φρονῶ ἐν θεῷ, ἀλλ’ ἐμαυτὸν μετρῶ, ἵνα μὴ ἐν καυχήσει ἀπόλωμαι. νῦν γάρ με δεῖ πλέον φοβεῖσθαι καὶ μὴ προσέχειν τοῖς φυσιοῦσίν με. οἱ γὰρ λέγοντές μοι μαστιγοῦσίν με.
ἀγαπῶ μὲν γὰρ τὸ παθεῖν, ἀλλ’ οὐκ οἶδα, εἰ ἄξιός εἰμι. τὸ γὰρ ζῆλος πολλοῖς μὲν οὐ φαίνεται, ἐμὲ δὲ πλέον πολεμεῖ. χρῄζω οὖν πραότητος, ἐν ᾗ καταλύεται ὁ ἄρχων τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου.
thought_title: Fear of boasting and the need for gentleness
orientation: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, is writing to the church in Tralles while being taken under guard to Rome, and here he reflects on his own spiritual state and the danger of pride.
pass_a_gloss: Many things I think in God, but myself I measure, in order that not in boasting I perish. For now me it is necessary more to fear and not to pay attention to those who puff me up. For those who speak to me whip me. I love indeed the suffering, but I do not know, whether worthy I am. For the zeal to many indeed does not appear, but me more it wars against. I need therefore gentleness, in which is destroyed the ruler of this age.

lemmas.gloss: I think, I have in mind

choices.why: The verb φυσιόω means to inflate or make proud; 'puff up' preserves the metaphor of inflation and the negative sense of pride.
The verb μαστιγόω means to whip or scourge; keeping 'whip' preserves the physical image of harm done by flattering speech.
The glossary gives 'passion' for πάθος, but here the infinitive παθεῖν refers to the act of suffering; 'the suffering' keeps the verbal force and connects to Ignatius's coming martyrdom.
The noun ζῆλος can mean zeal or jealousy; 'zeal' fits the context of Ignatius's eagerness for martyrdom, which he says is not visible to many but wars against him.
The noun πραότης means gentleness or meekness; 'gentleness' is the standard rendering and fits the contrast with the warlike zeal.
The verb καταλύω means to destroy or overthrow; the passive 'is destroyed' preserves the passive voice and the sense that the ruler of this age is brought down by gentleness.

pass_b_english: I have many thoughts in God, but I take my own measure, so that I do not perish through boasting. For now I must be more afraid, and not pay attention to those who puff me up. For those who speak to me whip me.

I do love the suffering, but I do not know whether I am worthy. For zeal is not visible to many, but it wars against me all the more. So I need gentleness, in which the ruler of this age is destroyed.

last_rejected.why: Brief glosses πάθος as 'passion'; τὸ παθεῖν should match, not 'suffering'.
last_rejected.fix: I do love to suffer, but I do not know whether I am worthy.
last_rejected.ruling: τὸ παθεῖν is articular infinitive of πάσχω ('to suffer'), not πάθος ('passion'); 'suffering' is correct.

last_rejected.quote: zeal is not visible to many
last_rejected.source_quote: τὸ γὰρ ζῆλος πολλοῖς μὲν οὐ φαίνεται
last_rejected.why: ζῆλος is 'envy/jealousy' not 'zeal'; φαίνεται is 'seem/appear' not 'be visible'
last_rejected.fix: For jealousy does not appear to many, but it wars against me all the more
last_rejected.ruling: ζῆλος means both 'zeal' and 'envy'; φαίνεται means 'appear/be visible'. Both renderings are within normal range.

problems.quote: For those who speak to me whip me
problems.why: 'Whip' as metaphor for flattery that wounds spiritually is obscure; modern reader thinks literal violence.
problems.fix: Consider 'lash me with their words' or add note on metaphor.

edits.old: For those who speak to me whip me.
edits.new: For those who speak to me lash me with their words.

problems.quote: For those who speak to me lash me with their words
problems.why: 'Lash me with their words' reads like a literal translation; meaning is unclear—flattery or criticism?
problems.fix: Clarify: likely means 'those who praise me are really whipping me' (i.e., tempting pride).

edits.old: For those who speak to me lash me with their words.
edits.new: For those who speak to me whip me.

fixed: The English already says exactly what the source says: 'For those who speak to me whip me.' The previous edit added 'with their words,' which was not in the source and made the meaning unclear. Reverting to the literal gloss is the smallest change that fixes the problem.
